title: Endpoint hardening, patching and backups
subtitle: Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services.
description: Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 5 — Endpoint hardening, patching and backups

LEARNING OUTCOME
Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Endpoints include laptops, phones, workstations and servers. Remove unnecessary software and services, standardize secure configurations, remove defaults, restrict local administrator rights and enable appropriate protection. A baseline provides a repeatable state to compare against.

blocks.text: Inventory systems, evaluate vendor guidance and exploitation evidence, prioritize exposure, test updates, deploy in waves and verify success. Track unsupported platforms as a risk needing migration, isolation or a documented plan. A deadline is meaningless if nobody measures whether updates installed.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Attack surface. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Backup tiers. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Keep separate protected copies and restrict who can modify or delete them. Test restores, record recovery time and recovery point objectives, and ensure backup credentials are not casually reachable from normal sessions. Recovery exercises include people and dependencies, not just files.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.question: What proves that a backup strategy works?
options: A successful restore test with measured recovery outcomes
The backup drive is always online
A backup job was scheduled once
blocks.explanation: A restore test validates recoverability, not just the existence of copies.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound patch-management process?
options: Inventory, prioritize, test, deploy and verify
Count patches but never confirm installation
blocks.explanation: Patch work is complete only after the deployed state is verified.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
Copy all customer records for convenience
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
